How to read this map

DC Standort is a screening map for AI data-centre sites in Germany. The country is cut into 3 747 cells of 10 × 10 km. For each one it estimates what the location adds to the cost of a project — the grid connection, the fibre trench, the yearly grid fee and the cost of placing the waste heat the law obliges you to reuse — and shows it in euros per megawatt-hour of electricity consumed. Everything is computed from your answers, in the browser, from public data of 20 September 2026.

How to use it

  • Describe your project. Megawatts of IT load, and what it may connect to: the nearest substation whatever its voltage, any 110 kV or any 220/380 kV substation, or only the Reifegrad nodes — the 106 substations where a transmission operator publishes free capacity and, for some, the year it frees up. Only that last choice knows dates, so by when counts only there. The rate and horizon under Cost of location turn the one-off investment into a yearly charge.
  • Read the map. Each cell is coloured by its cost; the grade A–E map puts the cells that pass your filters into five equal bands, A the cheapest fifth.
  • Click a cell. The profile lists every line of its cost with the source behind it, where its connection point is, the heat and fibre evidence, and the buildable land. The other maps under Colour by show one ingredient at a time; the Layers button draws the infrastructure itself.

What the cost includes, and what it does not

  • Included: the line to the connection point at the €/km of its voltage, one switching bay, the operator’s connection charge (BKZ), the fibre trench at 85 €/m, the 2026 grid fee at the voltage of that point — the uniform transmission tariff, or the local 110 kV operator’s price sheet — and the cost of placing your mandatory share of waste heat (10 % from 2026, 20 % from 2028).
  • Left out because they cost the same anywhere: your own substation, the building, the IT. It is a differential between locations, not a budget.
  • Not priced yet: cooling, land, water. The municipal trade tax is shown in the profile as a rate on profit, not added to the total.
  • Where a 110 kV operator publishes no price sheet, the fee is assumed at the 90th percentile of the published ones: a gap must never look cheap. The profile says why the sheet is missing.

What this is not

  • Not a site. A cell is 10 000 hectares. Nothing here says a parcel exists, is for sale, or can be permitted; the buildable-land map only says a 30 ha campus fits somewhere in the cell.
  • Not a ranking. Two cells whose cost ranges overlap — the profile shows them — are not ordered by the model. The grade is a band, and it is relative to the cells your filters leave in.
  • Not a heat-network map. For five cells in six the distance to heat is measured to a census cell with dwellings on district heating: evidence a network exists nearby, not a connection able to absorb 100 MW.
  • Not current beyond its snapshot. Published capacity is frozen at the date it was retrieved and hashed; operators revise it continuously. Grid fees are the 2026 price sheets, subsidy included; they are set yearly.

The index

  • Before the cost, the tool scored cells 0–1 on three distances — grid, fibre, heat — averaged with the weights at the bottom of the left column. It is kept under Colour by as a second view; it does not enter the cost.

About

  • Who. Built by Iñigo Baraia-Etxaburu as a master’s thesis at the Technical University of Munich. It is a research prototype shared with developers and grid planners for feedback; nothing here is advice.
  • Data. Public sources, retrieved 20 September 2026 and frozen; the sources table above says what may be redistributed. Grid fees are the 2026 price sheets. Published capacity changes continuously.
  • Feedback. What is wrong, what is missing, what you would need to trust a number: i.baraia@tum.de.
  • Where it lives. https://inigobaraia.github.io/dc-standort/ — the address always shows the latest version; whatever follows the # in the address bar reproduces your current view, so copy the whole address to share exactly what you see.
  • Tour. Show the one-minute tour again.
  • Version. Model V8 · page v62 · 3 747 cells of 10 × 10 km. Contains OpenStreetMap data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL.
